(2) TRUMP CALLED OFF THE WEEKEND STRIKES at the request of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, says a deal is 'imminent' and US-Iran negotiations START TODAY, with the headline term being the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT.' meta.regime: Two separate official actions are draining the two largest risk premia in FX at the same time, and both cut the same way. The first is monetary: Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama issued a statement on Monday confirming that the Ministry of Finance purchased yen IN COORDINATION WITH THE US TREASURY, and Trump confirmed it from Washington, saying Japan 'wanted a little bit of help' and that the US took a 'financial benefit' out of it. USD/JPY fell about 1% to 156.34 having been above 163 - a 40-year high - late last week. Overt acknowledgement of coordinated intervention is rare; the last comparable case was the 2011 earthquake operation. That converts the yen story from a fading unilateral defence into a G2 policy stance, and the MoF added it 'would not hesitate to act further.' The second is geopolitical: Trump called off the strikes he had promised for the weekend after Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE urged restraint, said a deal is 'imminent,' and confirmed US-Iran negotiations begin Monday - with the deal he described covering the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT' and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began on Feb 28. Markets have started to price it: WTI is near $84, Brent about $88, gold slipped 1.5% to $4,044 and DXY is at a six-week low of 99.96. The knock-on that most desks have not repriced yet is in the euro: the ~70% September ECB hike sitting in the curve was built on the oil surge Lagarde flagged as an upside inflation risk, so a reopened strait deflates the euro's only hawkish leg while euro-area annual growth is just 0.3%.
meta.nextBigEvent: US July employment report (Fri Aug 7, 12:30Z). Consensus is +91k after June's +57k, with unemployment expected at 4.3% from 4.2% and April-May already revised down 74k combined; TradingEconomics' own model is lower at +79k. A second sub-100k print kills the September hike the three July dissenters are pushing and breaks the dollar; a clean beat re-arms it and is the main threat to the yen longs. US July CPI on Aug 12 (TE forecast 3.4%) is the follow-up.

dailyRead: Today is defined by two official interventions, one monetary and one diplomatic, and they push the same way - out of risk premium. Start with the yen, because it is now the cleanest trade in the coverage by a distance. Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed on Monday in Tokyo that the Ministry of Finance bought yen IN COORDINATION WITH THE US TREASURY, and Trump confirmed it from the American side, saying Japan 'wanted a little bit of help, and we're always there for Japan' and that the US extracted a 'financial benefit' from the operation. USD/JPY dropped about 1% to 156.34 on the announcement, having traded above 163 - a 40-year high - as recently as late last week. This is a categorically different fact from Friday's read of a unilateral MoF defence that had merely held: a coordinated G2 operation with the world's reserve-currency issuer on the yen's side of the trade is the strongest possible official signal, it is openly acknowledged rather than 'suspected' (Astris' Neil Newman notes the last comparable case was 2011), and the MoF explicitly said it 'would not hesitate to act further.' It also means the US Treasury is voluntarily short dollars against yen, which is a policy-level dollar negative that no amount of September hike pricing offsets in this one cross. JPY goes to +3 and every XXX/JPY pair is a short; JPYBASKET is a HIGH-conviction long. The fundamentals behind it are cooperating too - the BoJ held 1.00% on Jul 31 with Takata dissenting for 1.25%, Tokyo July core CPI jumped to 1.9% from 1.6% with headline at 2.0%, June CPI is 1.7% with core 1.6%, jobs-to-applicants is back at 1.18, manufacturing PMI 54.7 and the 10-year JGB is at 2.80%. The one honest caveat: the July Outlook Report CUT FY2026 CPI to 2.5% from 2.8% and May wage growth slowed to 3.2% from 3.6%, so the BoJ is in no hurry - Sept 18 is a hold, Oct/Dec is the live meeting. Second, the war premium. Trump called off the weekend strikes he had threatened, at the request of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, said a deal is 'imminent' and confirmed US-Iran negotiations begin today - with the deal as he described it covering the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT' and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. That is a far bigger headline than Friday's Iran-Oman transit talks, because the strait has been effectively closed since the war started on Feb 28 and because early July - when traffic briefly flowed - saw WTI below $70. Today WTI is near $84 and Brent about $88, so there is a lot of premium left to come out if this lands. USOIL is upgraded to a HIGH-conviction short, gold flips from RANGE to SHORT at $4,044 after a 1.5% Sunday drop, and GER40 gets a double tailwind (cheaper energy input costs plus a softer ECB discount rate). The euro is where the second-order thinking pays. Markets carry roughly a 70% probability of an ECB hike on Sept 10, and that pricing was explicitly built on the oil surge - Lagarde warned renewed Middle East hostilities and the oil rebound posed upside risk to euro-area inflation, and it overrode the dovish tone officials struck at Sintra in early July. Reopen the strait and that leg deflates, leaving a euro with 2.8% HICP, 2.4% core, 0.0% q/q Q1 GDP and 0.3% annual growth. So EUR is downgraded to neutral: EUR/USD comes off LONG to RANGE, EUR/AUD to RANGE, but EUR/CHF stays a HIGH-conviction long because the franc is worse still. On the franc, Friday's flip is confirmed and extending - EUR/CHF is at fresh highs around 0.9332 and USD/CHF is above 0.8850, with MUFG calling the policy gap a reason for further CHF losses and TD tying the weakness to carry AND to falling gold. Cheaper gold is a direct franc negative, so de-escalation hits CHF twice. The SNB is at 0% with panellists seeing no change until 2027, June CPI is 0.5% with core 0.3% and producer/import prices deflating at -2.1%, and the Bank has only pledged to sell francs against APPRECIATION - it is content with the slide. CAD is the other clear short: StatCan's June CPI cooled to 2.8% from 3.2% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, BOTH BELOW the BoC's 2% target, gasoline decelerating to +20.5% y/y from +33.2%, and the Bank on its sixth consecutive hold at 2.25% since Jul 15 - and now the terms-of-trade leg is the thing being negotiated away in Tehran. USD/CAD flips from RANGE to LONG. Two upgrades to note. AUD is less broken than the last two files implied: the Q2 weighted median actually ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, July PMIs printed six-month highs (manufacturing 51.7, services 53.0, composite 52.6), and while all four major banks expect a hold on Aug 11, Finder's survey has 55% of economists seeing at least one more hike in 2026 and TE's own model carries 4.60%. AUD moves up to neutral and AUD/CHF, AUD/CAD go long. NZD keeps the only executed tightening path (2.50% since Jul 8, TE models 2.75% by Sept 2) with two-year inflation expectations at 2.53%, a five-month high in ANZ business confidence at 56.1 and Q2 CPI at 4.1% - but its hawkish case is the MOST oil-dependent in the coverage, because the RBNZ's own July statement credited a partial Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation. A total reopening is precisely the scenario that lets them pause. So NZD longs get downgraded conviction and AUD/NZD comes down to LOW-MED. Sterling is the quiet winner among the Europeans: the BoE's 6-3 hold on Jul 30 still stands, employment was +148k in May with wages at 4.3% and unemployment down to 4.9%, and July PMIs jumped hard - services to 51.8 from 48.8, composite to 52.1 from 49.3. GBP/CHF, GBP/CAD and GBP/AUD are the expressions; GBP/JPY is still a short because the yen leg is stronger. On the dollar: Q2 GDP came in at 1.5% (advance, Jul 30) after 2.1% in Q1, June CPI is 3.5% with core down to 2.6%, June PCE 3.7%/3.3% and payrolls +57k - yet the Fed held on Jul 29 with three dissents for a hike, Warsh refused to give guidance, and CME FedWatch still carries roughly 56-61% of a September hike (TE reads it closer to 77%). DXY at 99.96 is a six-week low. Lean short USD only where the other leg is doing the work. The governing risk cuts hard both ways: these Iran talks have collapsed repeatedly, and a breakdown would snap oil, gold, CAD and the whole CHF block back within a session - while conversely a hot payrolls print on Friday is the one thing that can fight a joint US-Japan intervention.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent for a hike against a consensus of 7-2. June CPI 2.6% with core 2.6% and services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wage growth 4.3%, unemployment down to 4.9% - and July PMIs jumped: services 51.8 from 48.8, composite 52.1 from 49.3. TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%.

JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. But the July Outlook Report CUT FY2026 CPI to 2.5% from 2.8% while raising FY2026 GDP to 0.6% and FY2027 CPI to 2.4% - so the Bank is not in a rush, and May wage growth slowed to 3.2% from 3.6%. Tamura wants the rate at a neutral ~2% via 25bp every few months. The near-term yen driver is fiscal, not monetary: a joint MoF/US Treasury operation with an explicit pledge to act again.

AUD.note: Cash rate 4.35% after three hikes in 2026 (Feb, Mar, May) on the energy shock. Q2 trimmed mean 3.6% but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%. All four major banks expect a hold; Finder's survey has 55% of economists seeing at least one more hike in 2026 and TE's model carries 4.60% for August and 4.85% by Sept 29 - the hawkish tail is alive even if August is not the meeting.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, with further increases described as possible. Q2 CPI 4.1% (fuel-led, petrol +27.5%), two-year inflation expectations up to 2.53% and one-year to 3.41%, ANZ business confidence 56.1 - a five-month high. The catch: the RBNZ's own July statement credited the PARTIAL Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation, so a total reopening is the scenario that lets them pause.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; Bloomberg-surveyed panellists see no change until 2027. June CPI 0.5% y/y with 0.0% m/m and core 0.3%; producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y. The June statement flagged a readiness to intervene against rapid APPRECIATION - the SNB is content to let the franc slide, and FX reserves jumped CHF 47.9bn in June. Swiss July CPI is due Aug 4.

catalysts.event: US-Iran negotiations OPEN TODAY — 'Complete and Total' Hormuz reopening on the table
catalysts.note: Trump called off the strikes he had promised for the weekend after Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE urged restraint, said a deal is 'imminent' and confirmed negotiations begin Monday. He described the deal as covering the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT' and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began Feb 28; when traffic briefly flowed in early July WTI traded below $70 against ~$84 now. Against that: Iran struck two tankers under US air escort on Jul 31, launched drones at the Ahmad al-Jaber base in Kuwait, and US-Saudi strikes in Iraq killed about 20 militants including five IRGC members. This is the two-way swing factor over oil, gold, CAD, NZD and the entire CHF block.

catalysts.event: Joint US-Japan FX intervention — MoF says it will not hesitate to act again
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed on Aug 3 that the MoF purchased yen in coordination with the US Treasury; Trump confirmed it from Washington. USD/JPY fell ~1% to 156.34 from above 163 late last week. Overt acknowledgement of coordinated intervention is rare - the last comparable case was 2011 - and it converts a fading unilateral defence into standing G2 policy. Size yen shorts for a second operation against you; size yen longs for a squeeze if the pair drifts back toward 160.

geopolitics: The war premium is being negotiated away in real time, and today is the day it gets tested. Trump called off the strikes he had promised for the weekend after Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates urged restraint, said publicly that a deal is 'imminent,' and confirmed that US-Iran negotiations begin Monday. The deal he described covers the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT' and an end to Iran's nuclear threat - a far larger prize than the Iran-Oman transit talks that were the story on Friday, because the strait has been effectively closed by Iran since the war began on Feb 28 and roughly 20% of global oil shipments normally transit it. The counter-evidence is still ugly: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Jul 31 it had struck two tankers attempting to pass under US 'aerial escort' and turned four others back; Iran launched drones at the Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait, which Kuwait says it intercepted; US and Saudi forces struck Iran-aligned militia positions in Iraq killing about 20, including five IRGC members; CENTCOM has redirected 24 commercial vessels since restarting its blockade of Iranian ports; and the Senate again rejected an effort to limit the President's war powers, 49-50, in what is likely the last such vote before the Aug 10 recess. FX transmission: (1) Crude is the channel and it has the most room of anything on the board - WTI near $84 and Brent near $88 against sub-$70 in early July when traffic briefly flowed - so USOIL is upgraded to a HIGH-conviction short. (2) CAD is the primary currency casualty: with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% below the BoC's target, the terms-of-trade bid was its only support and it is the thing being traded away. (3) Gold flips from RANGE to SHORT at $4,044 after a 1.5% Sunday drop; silver at $58-59 stays a RANGE because de-escalation helps its industrial leg. (4) The franc is hit twice - it loses the haven bid and it loses the gold correlation TD identifies as a driver - so the entire CHF block stays short-franc. (5) NZD is the surprise loser: the RBNZ's July statement explicitly credited a PARTIAL Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation, so a total reopening is the Bank's own stated off-ramp from the September hike. (6) The euro is the non-obvious one: the ~70% September ECB hike in the curve was built on the oil surge Lagarde flagged, so a reopening deflates the euro's only hawkish leg. (7) The yen is the one currency immune to all of it, because its bid is official and bilateral rather than geopolitical. (8) Size everything for a snap-back: these talks have collapsed repeatedly, and a breakdown would reverse oil, gold, CAD, NZD and the CHF crosses inside a single session.
